passage: Joseph, 24, leans into the community-radio microphone. 'You asked who I look up to. Honestly? Uma Aunty, our choir leader. She's seventy-one. Last Christmas she taught the wrong harmony for a whole week, and when the youngest singer pointed it out, she stopped, laughed and said, "You're right, I've been leading you all into a ditch." Then she asked the kid to show everyone. She asks us younger ones what songs we want. She listens even when we're half-joking. Compare that with the committee member who shouts "Respect your elders!" at us. We nod at him and roll our eyes once he's gone. For Uma Aunty, nobody has to be told. We just stand up when she walks in.'

qa.q: How old is Uma Aunty?
qa.a: She's seventy-one.

qa.q: What does Joseph feel towards Uma Aunty, and why?
qa.a: Joseph feels deep admiration and warmth, because she admits her mistakes, asks the younger singers' opinions and truly listens.

qa.q: What could the committee member learn from Uma Aunty?
qa.a: That respect comes from listening and owning mistakes, not from demanding it; shouting only earns eye-rolls behind his back.

qa.q: How might the youngest singer have felt when Uma Aunty admitted the mistake?
qa.a: The singer probably felt proud and valued, since speaking up was welcomed and even turned into a chance to lead.

grounding: Shows a junior who watches an elder admit errors, ask opinions and listen, and gives that elder real respect unasked, while demanded respect earns only hidden eye-rolling.

passage:
From my desk opposite the chief sub-editor's, I've watched Harish-da for eight months. He's fifty-eight and has been at the paper longer than I've been alive. Yesterday a trainee pointed out that his headline had the wrong district name. The room went silent. Harish-da took off his glasses, read it again, and said, 'Good catch. Fix it, and put your initials on it.' At the Monday meeting he asks the youngest reporters first which stories matter, then listens with his chin on his hand. I can't tell what he's thinking behind that calm face. I just know that when he walks in, we all sit up, and nobody ever told us to.
Anirban

qa.q: What did Harish-da tell the trainee to do?
qa.a: 'Fix it, and put your initials on it.'

qa.q: What does Anirban feel towards Harish-da, and what shows it?
qa.a: Anirban feels admiration and respect, shown by sitting up when Harish-da walks in without ever being told to.

qa.q: What could a new senior learn from how Harish-da handled the wrong district name?
qa.a: To admit the error calmly and credit the person who caught it; that earns lasting respect instead of fear.

qa.q: Why might Harish-da choose to ask the youngest reporters first?
qa.a: He may believe fresh eyes see what he misses and want them to know their views count, though Anirban can only guess his thoughts.

grounding: Illustrates a junior colleague watching an elder who admits mistakes, asks the young for opinions and listens, and giving that elder real respect without being told.

passage:
Week one: At the site office in Nagpur, Shreya ma'am, the oldest engineer on the project, stopped the review. "My load figures on sheet four are wrong. I've corrected them. Please check my maths." Hemant, three months into the job, blinked. Senior people didn't say that.

Week three: Before deciding on the scaffolding, she turned to the juniors first. "Hemant, you were on site yesterday. What did you see?" He answered, and she used it.

Week six: In the canteen, the others were laughing about the regional head who made everyone stand when he walked in, mimicking his "Do you know who I am?"

Someone started on Shreya ma'am. Hemant put his tray down. "Not her. She listens." Nobody argued.

qa.q: Which sheet had the wrong load figures?
qa.a: Her load figures on sheet four were wrong.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when Shreya ma'am admitted her error?
qa.a: Hemant was surprised and quietly impressed, since senior people didn't say that.

qa.q: What could other seniors learn from Shreya ma'am?
qa.a: Admit errors openly and ask juniors what they saw; that earns respect that lasts, unlike making people stand up.

qa.q: How might the regional head be seen by the juniors?
qa.a: The juniors obey him outwardly but mock him in the canteen, so his demanded respect is hollow.

grounding: Shows a junior who comes to respect an elder who admits errors and asks opinions, while demanded respect draws hidden mockery.

passage:
Rajni, you asked why I still keep a photo of old Kulkarni-sir on my desk. Let me, Jaya, tell you.

In 1989 I joined the textile mill in Solapur as the youngest clerk, twenty-three and terrified. The manager before him made us stand when he entered and shouted when we were late. We bowed to his face and drew cartoons of him in the tea room.

Then Kulkarni-sir came. In his first week he sat with us at lunch and asked, "What is broken here? Tell me honestly." When I pointed out an error in his wage sheet, he said, "Thank you, Jaya. I was wrong," in front of everyone.

Nobody told us to respect him. We just did. When he retired, the whole floor cried, even the loom men who never cried at anything.

qa.q: Where did Jaya work in 1989?
qa.a: Jaya joined the textile mill in Solapur as the youngest clerk.

qa.q: How did young Jaya feel about the earlier manager?
qa.a: Jaya was terrified of him, bowing to his face while the clerks mocked him with cartoons in the tea room.

qa.q: What turning point made Jaya respect Kulkarni-sir?
qa.a: When Jaya pointed out an error in his wage sheet and he said thank you and admitted he was wrong in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Kulkarni-sir have felt at his retirement, seeing the floor cry?
qa.a: He probably felt moved and valued, knowing the respect was given freely rather than demanded.

grounding: Shows a junior who gives real respect to an elder who listens and admits errors, compared with a demanding manager who was mocked behind his back.

passage:
Twenty minutes to the print deadline, and the power in the Lucknow newsroom flickered off, then on. Half the screens rebooted.

Anand-sir, sixty and the oldest editor on the floor, didn't shout. He pulled a chair into the middle. "Front page. We have one story too many. Vikas, you checked the flood figures. Are they solid?"

Vikas swallowed. "Sir, the district number is from yesterday. It's higher now."

Anand-sir read it again. "You're right. I missed that. Change it, and put your name on the correction note."

They made the deadline with ninety seconds to spare.

At two a.m., waiting for his auto, Vikas realised he would do anything that man asked, and nobody had ever told him to.

qa.q: How long before the deadline did the power flicker?
qa.a: Twenty minutes to the print deadline.

qa.q: What did Vikas realise while waiting for his auto, and what feeling does it show?
qa.a: Vikas realised he would do anything Anand-sir asked, showing a deep admiration and trust that nobody had demanded.

qa.q: What could a young editor copy from Anand-sir under pressure?
qa.a: Stay calm, ask the person who checked the facts, admit a miss openly and give credit, even with minutes left.

qa.q: How might Anand-sir see the moment he admitted the mistake?
qa.a: Anand-sir probably sees it as ordinary accuracy work, not a loss of face, which is why he said it so easily.

grounding: Shows a junior who comes to respect an older editor who listens, asks opinions and admits errors under deadline pressure, without being told to.

passage: At the Pune architecture firm, Pema, twenty-four, noticed who people really respected. The founding partner demanded "sir" and interrupted everyone; behind his back, juniors did impressions of his lectures at lunch. But Zainab ma'am, the senior partner who was nearly sixty, was different. In Monday meetings she asked the youngest people first. When Pema pointed out a staircase measurement she had got wrong, Zainab ma'am said, "Good catch. I was wrong," in front of the client. She remembered everyone's names, even the tea boy's daughter's. Nobody told Pema to respect her. Pema just did, completely. When Zainab ma'am asked for volunteers to stay late for a deadline, half the office raised their hands, Pema first. Nobody did impressions of her. Pema wrote in her notebook: be like ma'am when I'm old.

qa.q: What did Zainab ma'am say when Pema pointed out the measurement error?
qa.a: "Good catch. I was wrong."

qa.q: How did Pema feel about Zainab ma'am, and what shows it?
qa.a: Pema felt deep admiration and respect, volunteering first to stay late and writing in the notebook to be like her.

qa.q: What does Zainab ma'am do that earns real respect?
qa.a: She asks juniors first, admits her errors openly and remembers people's names, so respect comes freely rather than being demanded.

qa.q: How might the juniors see the founding partner compared with Zainab ma'am?
qa.a: They obey him on the surface but mock him in private, while they genuinely respect Zainab ma'am and volunteer for her.

grounding: It illustrates a junior who watches an elder listen, admit errors and ask opinions, and gives real respect without being told.
